paragraphs.heading: A dynasty you can dig up
paragraphs.text: The Shang dynasty, also called the Yin dynasty, was a royal house that ruled in the Yellow River valley in the 2nd millennium BC. Tradition places it after the Xia dynasty and before the Western Zhou. Modern scholars date it from the 16th to the 11th century BC, and they agree more about when it ended than when it began. It is the earliest dynasty in traditional Chinese history that archaeology firmly backs up.

paragraphs.heading: The last capital
paragraphs.text: The site of Yinxu, near today's city of Anyang, was the final Shang capital, called Yin. Digging there has uncovered eleven large royal tombs and the foundations of palace buildings. It has also turned up the remains of animals and people who were killed as offerings in state ceremonies. Tens of thousands of objects in bronze, jade, stone, bone and pottery have come out of the ground.

paragraphs.heading: Oracle bones
paragraphs.text: Yinxu's greatest find is the earliest known Chinese writing. Most of it is divination texts carved on oracle bones, which were usually turtle shells or the shoulder blades of oxen. The first scientific digs in the 1920s and 1930s found more than 20,000 of them, and over four times that number have been found since. These texts shed light on Shang politics, economy, religion, art and medicine.

paragraphs.heading: What later writers said
paragraphs.text: The traditional story of the Shang comes from books such as the Book of Documents, the Bamboo Annals and the Shiji. The Han historian Sima Qian put together a timeline of the Shang in the Shiji, around 91 BC. He tells some events in detail but only places others in a certain king's reign. The Bamboo Annals give a slightly different account, and the surviving copies are of disputed authenticity. In the last century, Wang Guowei showed that the order of Shang kings matched Sima Qian's list.

paragraphs.heading: Shang or Yin
paragraphs.text: The Shang have long also been known as Yin, a name used for both the dynasty and its last capital. Since the 3rd century AD, Yin has often meant just the later half of the Shang, and it is the main name for the dynasty in Japan, Korea and Vietnam. The name seems to have come from the Zhou, who ruled afterwards. The oracle bones themselves call the state Shang and its capital the Great Settlement of Shang.

paragraphs.heading: Founding myth and fall
paragraphs.text: In the founding myth, a woman named Jiandi swallowed an egg dropped by a black bird and gave birth to Xie. Xie helped Yu the Great tame a great flood and was given a place called Shang as a reward. Thirteen generations later his descendant Tang overthrew Jie, the cruel last Xia ruler. The Shang moved their capital five times, and the last move, to Yin under King Pan Geng, began the dynasty's golden age. The last king, Di Xin, is said to have killed himself after Wu of Zhou defeated his army.

paragraphs.heading: After the conquest
paragraphs.text: King Wu of Zhou let Di Xin's son, Wu Geng, rule the Shang as a dependent kingdom. After King Wu died, the Shang joined a revolt known as the Rebellion of the Three Guards, which collapsed after three years and left the Zhou in control. A brother of Di Xin was later made Duke of Song. The dukes of Song honoured the Shang kings with rites until 286 BC, when Qi conquered Song, and Confucius may have descended from the Shang kings through them.
